passage: Collectors of early printed maps pay premiums for period color, applied when a map was first published, over color added later. Dating the printing of a map is usually straightforward, since publishers recorded their editions. The coloring is another matter. Pigment might have been applied in the publisher's workshop the week the sheet was printed, by an owner's colorist a generation later, or by a nineteenth-century dealer brightening old stock. Paper takes a wash of color at any age and carries no date. A map's edition date therefore settles when the sheet was printed and nothing more. It follows that a cataloger who records the date of printing as the date of the coloring ______
question: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: will err, if at all, by making the coloring seem more recent than it is, since many sheets were colored before printing.
can rely on the attribution being sound, because publishers' edition records listed which copies had been colored in the workshop.
has adopted the only defensible convention, since no evidence of any kind can distinguish early coloring from later additions.
risks describing the color as older than it is, since pigment may have been applied years or even centuries after printing.

explanation:
**Choice D is correct.** The printing date is the earliest possible moment the color could have been applied — every alternative the passage lists (an owner's colorist a generation on, a nineteenth-century dealer) comes later. Equating the two dates therefore errs in one direction only: it makes the color look older than it may be.

**The Full Solution:**
- A sheet cannot be colored before it exists, so the printing date is a floor for the coloring date, never a ceiling.
- The passage's examples of later coloring — a generation later, or a nineteenth-century dealer brightening old stock — show how far above that floor the true date can sit.
- Recording the floor as the actual date collapses that gap in one direction: the recorded age of the color can only be too great, never too small. That is D's conclusion.

**Why the other choices are wrong:**
- A: It runs the error backward and rests on an impossibility — sheets colored before they were printed.
- B: It contradicts the passage, whose edition records date printings; the text says the paper "carries no date" for color.
- C: It overreaches twice — the passage never calls the convention defensible, and "no evidence of any kind" goes far beyond what the catalogers' caution implies.
